title: Your Strategy Reviews Are Status Meetings in Disguise
author: Make Better Strategy
summary: This essay from the Make Better Strategy newsletter argues that most strategy reviews only ever answer two questions—are we executing the plan, and are the numbers moving—and that this makes them functionally indistinguishable from ordinary status meetings. The author's central claim is that a review only earns the name if it also tests two harder questions: are the strategy's founding assumptions still true, and does the team still believe in the plan. To operationalize this, the piece proposes a four-part rhythm called ARIS (Action, Results, Insights, Spirit), arguing that skipping the Insights and Spirit stages leaves leaders unable to tell an execution problem from a wrong strategic bet, two failures that demand opposite responses. The piece closes by reframing the review itself: not a compliance check on whether people did their homework, but a learning mechanism for catching a wrong bet while it is still cheap to change course.
points: Introduces the ARIS framework (Action, Results, Insights, Spirit) as a diagnostic rhythm for strategy reviews, arguing most reviews stop at the first two and never test whether assumptions or team buy-in still hold.

Argues that tracking only Action and Results makes it impossible to distinguish an execution failure from a strategic-hypothesis failure, leading leaders to either push harder on a broken bet or abandon a sound strategy too early.
Reframes strategy reviews as learning mechanisms rather than control mechanisms — the goal is to find out if you're still right, not to audit compliance.
Names 'Spirit' as the review's most avoided question — whether the team still believes in the strategy — arguing that quiet disengagement kills a strategy before it is formally declared dead.
quotes: Because there are two more questions a real strategy review has to ask, and most reviews never get near them. Are our original assumptions still valid? And: Does anyone still actually believe in this?
We've gotten very good at tracking activity and results — dashboards, RAG statuses, quarterly business reviews. We've gotten very bad at asking the two questions that dashboards can't answer.
Insights. Are our assumptions still valid? This is the question that separates a review from a status meeting.

If you only track Action and Results, you cannot tell the difference between two completely different failures: an execution problem (we have the right strategy but we're not delivering it) and a strategic-hypothesis failure (we're delivering beautifully on a strategy that was wrong).
A review isn't a control mechanism — a place to check whether people did their homework. It's a learning mechanism — a place to find out whether you're still right, and to adapt while it's cheap.

Spirit asks the unaskable in most cultures: does anyone in this room still actually believe in this, or are we going through the motions? A strategy no one believes in is already over; it just hasn't been declared yet.
